column3: Near-verbatim personal confession: calling on one's Lord entails associating none with Him.
The nearby command to hold to the Lord's unalterable words frames exclusive reliance before the parable.
Explicitly identifies associating partners with God as a grave false claim and sin.
The garden owner later repeats the focus's exact confession in regret after his wealth is destroyed.
The same section contrasts Lord-directed devotion with attraction to worldly adornment, developed in the parable.
Directly describes believers as those who do not associate partners with their Lord.
Moses seeks refuge in his and his opponents' one Lord, a related confession of sole protection.
The immediate context presents the Lord's truth and the consequences of belief or denial.
Names associators but does not develop the focus's personal confession of exclusive lordship.
Sincere servitude to God broadly supports undivided devotion but lacks the anti-association claim.
The immediate sequel promises that God does not waste the reward of faithful good action.
The categorical declaration that God has no partner closely states the focus's central claim.
Trust in Allah as my Lord and your Lord supports the focus's exclusive reliance on Him.
The local reward of lasting gardens contrasts with the garden owner's misplaced confidence in temporal wealth.
God's universal lordship supplies a broad theological basis for calling Him my Lord.
Combines Allah is my Lord and your Lord with a direct warning against associating partners.
Introduces the two-garden parable whose wealthy speaker is corrected by the focus.
The question of who is Lord establishes a general lordship theme without the focus's anti-association content.
Joins worship of Allah alone, refusal to associate partners, calling on Him, and return to Him.
Establishes the abundant gardens that lead the owner to the pride corrected in the focus.
Questions the authority behind association, but is less direct than the focus's personal rejection.
Inherited association is relevant broadly, though not the focus's immediate wealth-and-reliance setting.
The owner's boast of greater wealth and followers supplies the pride answered by the focus.
Human ingratitude toward his Lord is a broad moral backdrop, not a close association parallel.
Moses seeks refuge in his and his opponents' Lord, supporting exclusive dependence amid arrogance.
The garden owner's self-wronging claim that his garden will never perish immediately motivates the focus's reply.
Confesses one God and disavows what others associate with Him, closely paralleling the focus.
The exact declaration that Allah is my Lord and your Lord turns recognition into exclusive worship.
The owner's denial of the Hour and presumption of a better return expose the confidence challenged in the focus.
The future demand to produce alleged partners confirms their unreality and supports the focus's refusal.
Abraham rejects fear of associated powers while affirming his Lord's encompassing knowledge.
The immediate preceding rebuke of disbelief leads directly into the focus's confession.
Warns that many profess belief while associating partners, sharpening the need for explicit disavowal.
In the same surah, God shares His judgment with no one, reinforcing the focus's exclusive lordship.
The immediate continuation teaches the garden owner to attribute will and power to Allah alone.
Rejects powerless alleged intercessors and exalts God above what people associate with Him.
The self-reproaching soul does not clarify exclusive lordship or association.
The companion predicts the garden's collapse, validating his refusal to treat wealth as secure power.
Forbids taking Iblis and his descendants as allies besides God, a related rejection of rival allegiance.
Speculation about the Companions' number does not clarify the focus's confession.
The threatened loss of the garden's water continues the local exposure of wealth's fragility.
Joseph's inherited monotheism explicitly rejects associating anything with God.
The household-entry rule is an incidental match on 'anyone.'
After loss, the owner has no party to help him besides God and cannot save himself.
Naming the Lord of Moses and Aaron is a limited confession of lordship without an anti-association claim.
God's exhaustive knowledge is theologically compatible but not a close neighbour of the focus.
The parable concludes that true authority belongs to God alone, confirming the focus's claim.
A false future denial of association contrasts with the focus but offers limited positive support.
The afterlife dispute between followers and leaders does not closely address the focus.
Reward from the Lord is too general to clarify exclusive lordship or association.
Revelation and rejection are broadly related to guidance but not to the focus's central confession.
Turning wholly to the Creator while refusing association closely parallels undivided devotion.
The declaration that Allah alone is God grounds the focus's personal statement of exclusive lordship.
The demand to locate alleged associates exposes the emptiness rejected in the focus.
Allah alone as the Living, Self-Subsisting God provides a direct monotheistic foundation.
Glorifying the name of the great Lord is related devotion but does not address association.
Allah's absolute oneness concisely underwrites the refusal to associate anyone with Him.
Association and the Prophet's non-guardianship over others are only indirectly related to the focus.
Near-verbatim declaration: belief entails associating no one with our Lord.
The challenge to produce alleged partners confirms the focus's refusal to recognize them.
The separation of worship marks exclusive allegiance, though it lacks the Lord-and-association formula.
Sharing punishment is unrelated to the theological refusal of shirk.
The repeated separation of worship reinforces exclusive allegiance without the focus's exact language.
Partnership in Moses's mission is a different, legitimate sense of sharing.
Allah alone as protector and best helper supports reliance on Him rather than rival supports.
Again challenges alleged partners to appear, reinforcing their invalidity.
Gratitude for divine protection is general and lacks the focus's association theme.
The mention of associators in a statement about the religion's prevalence is too indirect.
Commands worship of Allah alone, the positive action corresponding to the focus's refusal.
Abraham's monotheistic way rejects association, though the context concerns sectarian claims.
The Lord's unfailing knowledge is a broad attribute rather than a close association parallel.
Rejects any protector other than Allah and explicitly forbids being among associators.
Affirms that even the named star Sirius is under the Lord's authority, countering rival powers.
Confessing the Lord of Moses and Aaron is related lordship language but not a close thematic parallel.
The reference to 'my lord' concerns Joseph's benefactor in a distinct moral narrative.
Calls to Allah with insight and explicitly disavows association, closely echoing the focus.
Seeking forgiveness from my Lord is a general devotional reference only.
Universal lordship over heavens, earth, and horizons supports the focus's claim of one Lord.
Shows how human religious authorities can be elevated into rival lords, illuminating practical association.
Marriage with associators has a related boundary but does not clarify the focus's confession.
The surah's closing restates one God and prohibits associating anyone in worship of one's Lord.
The magicians' return to our Lord supports exclusive ultimate allegiance under pressure.
Migration to my Lord expresses personal allegiance but not the focus's anti-association claim.
The Lord of all realms grounds the focus's exclusive naming of Allah as Lord.
The statement that the discourse is not jest does not relate to exclusive lordship.
Rejects another god besides Allah and exalts Him above all association.
Fearing no one except Allah gives a practical form of undivided allegiance.
A plea for increased punishment in Hell does not clarify the focus's themes.
Love of prolonged life among associators is a distant thematic connection.
Return to our Lord is a general confession without the focus's anti-association emphasis.
God's creative lordship, sovereignty, and sole divinity directly support exclusive devotion.
The messengers invoke their Lord's knowledge, but the mission claim is not a close neighbour.
The general command to fear Allah and obey the messenger lacks the focus's distinctive themes.
Exclusive inclination to Allah and refusal of association vividly portray the alternative affirmed in the focus.
The phrase 'Allah's kindled fire' does not clarify lordship or association.
God's incomparable majesty is explicitly set above what people associate with Him.
Following desire without knowledge is a broad moral overlap, not a direct association parallel.
God's sole divine kingship and transcendence above association strongly reinforce exclusive lordship.
The prohibition on giving for increase does not clarify the focus's confession.
The skewed allocation of goods between Allah and alleged partners concretely exposes the false association rejected in the focus.
Declares one God alone, supplying the core monotheistic basis for the focus's personal confession.
God, the angels, and people of knowledge testify that there is no god but Him, confirming exclusive divinity.
Calls all parties to worship none but Allah and not associate anything with Him.
Commands worship of Allah and association of nothing with Him, directly matching the focus's refusal.
States that associating partners with Allah is a grave straying, reinforcing the focus's explicit disavowal.
Names Allah as the Creator and sole God, then commands worship of Him alone.
Explicitly commands: do not associate anything with Him.
Rejects seeking any lord other than Allah, a close counterpart to calling Allah alone my Lord.
Forbids associating with Allah anything for which He gave no authority.
Challenges alleged partners to guide to truth, exposing why none can share the Lord's role.
Contrasts Allah's lordship over heaven and earth with powerless protectors and alleged partners.
Challenges whether there can be doubt about Allah, Creator of the heavens and earth.
Condemns setting equals alongside Allah, directly opposing the focus's undivided allegiance.
Affirms one God and contrasts this with hearts that deny the hereafter in arrogance.
Forbids taking two gods: He is one God alone.
Forbids setting another god alongside Allah, the direct negative counterpart to the focus.
Repeats the prohibition against another god alongside Allah in the concluding wisdoms.
Praises God who has no partner in dominion, clarifying the exclusive sovereignty confessed in the focus.
The Companions declare the Lord of heavens and earth and refuse ever to invoke another god besides Him.
Condemns a people's adoption of gods besides Allah, a close same-surah contrast to the focus.
As Lord of the heavens and earth, God is to be worshipped steadfastly and has no equal namesake.
Allah declares that there is no god but Him and commands worship and remembrance.
Identifies Allah alone as God, whose knowledge encompasses all things.
Argues that multiple gods in heaven and earth would have brought corruption, supporting divine singularity.
The message of every messenger is that there is no god but Allah, so worship Him.
Denies that any god exists alongside Allah and refutes divided divine dominion.
Affirms that Allah has no partner in dominion and created everything in due measure.
Praises servants who do not invoke another god with Allah.
Forbids invoking another god alongside Allah.
Declares Allah alone to be God and Lord of the supreme throne.
Names Allah as the sole God to whom all praise and judgment belong.
Forbids invoking another god alongside Allah and affirms that all judgment returns to Him.
Forbids obeying parents when they press one to associate with Allah what one has no knowledge of.
Uses a human ownership analogy to reject imagined partners in what Allah provides.
Luqman explicitly calls associating partners with Allah a tremendous wrong.
Challenges alleged gods besides Allah, who possess no share in heaven or earth.
Asks whether any creator besides Allah provides from heaven and earth, affirming sole lordship.
Challenges alleged partners to show what they created or what share they possess.
Rejects taking gods besides the Merciful because their intercession and protection cannot avail.
Records the arrogant rejection of the declaration that there is no god but Allah, making the central confession explicit.
Commands sincere religion for Allah alone and rejects taking intermediaries besides Him.
Affirms Allah as Creator and challenges the efficacy of powers invoked besides Him.
Contrasts belief when Allah alone is invoked with disbelief when partners are associated with Him.
Names Allah as Lord, Creator, and the only God, directly grounding the focus's confession.
Forbids worshipping those invoked besides Allah and commands submission to the Lord of all worlds.
Forbids prostration to the sun and moon and commands worship of their Creator alone.
Challenges whether any gods besides the Most Merciful were ever appointed for worship.
Challenges alleged partners to show what they created or share in creation.
Forbids placing another god alongside Allah.
Abraham and his followers declare disavowal of worship besides Allah and exclusive belief in Him.
Declares Allah alone as God and commands believers to place their trust in Him.
The mosques belong to Allah, so no one is to be invoked alongside Him; this is an especially close worship parallel.
Condemns taking equals besides Allah and loving them as Allah should be loved, exposing divided allegiance.
The Prophet is forbidden from worshipping those invoked besides Allah, directly paralleling exclusive devotion.
Abraham rejects taking idols as gods, a personal refusal of rival worship.
Challenges alleged partners to originate and restore creation, testing their supposed divine role.
Joseph contrasts multiple separate lords with Allah, the One, the Irresistible.
Only Allah answers truly; those invoked besides Him cannot answer, undermining rival dependence.
Rejects worship of powers besides Allah that control neither provision nor anything else.
Challenges those called besides Allah to remove harm or change it, exposing their powerlessness.
On the Day of Judgment, alleged partners cannot answer or help their callers, extending the surah's anti-association theme.
Condemns calling on what can neither harm nor benefit besides Allah.
Declares that whoever invokes another god alongside Allah has no proof and faces final accountability.
Condemns taking gods besides Allah that create nothing and cannot control benefit, harm, death, or life.
After signs of creation and provision, repeatedly asks whether there is a god with Allah.
The command to call alleged partners exposes their failure to answer on the Day of Judgment.
In danger people call on Allah with sincere devotion, revealing His sole claim to worship.
The angels deny that people truly worshipped them, exposing mistaken objects of association.
Notes that people take gods besides Allah hoping for help, a false reliance countered by the focus.
Rejects fabricated gods besides Allah, the Lord of all worlds.
Contrasts aversion when Allah alone is mentioned with delight in those invoked besides Him.
Warns that association would nullify one's deeds, underscoring the gravity of the focus's refusal.
Declares that the God is one God and commands upright orientation toward Him.
Rejects partners who legislate a religion Allah did not authorize, extending association to rival authority.
